pages.title: Judicial questions and Lord Bryce on governance
pages.summary: The page lists examination questions concerning judicial activism, judicial review, constitutional mandates, and judicial reforms. It introduces the topic with Lord Bryce's assertion that the functioning of the judicial system is the best test of a government's excellence and vital for good governance.

pages.title: Role of judiciary and constitutional active nature
pages.summary: The judiciary ensures that democracy does not become a tyranny of the majority through judicial review and the rule of law. Thinkers including Granville Austin and Pandit Nehru highlight the judiciary's active role in India's social revolution, supported by Article 36 defining the judiciary as part of the state.

pages.title: Articles 141 and 129: Supreme Court powers
pages.summary: Under Article 141, the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding across all courts until the legislature enacts legislation, as seen in the Vishakha guidelines. The Constitution establishes a fiercely independent judiciary with Article 129 designating the Supreme Court as a court of record possessing contempt powers.

pages.title: Supreme Court powers and jurisdiction
pages.summary: Articles 137, 142, and 144 grant the Supreme Court powers to review its orders, do complete justice, and bind all civil and judicial authorities to act in its aid. The page also outlines the Court's federal, advisory, writ, and restricted appellate jurisdictions.

pages.title: Supreme Court independence and Upendra Baxi's assessment
pages.summary: The independence of the Supreme Court is maintained through stringent removal procedures and salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Scholars like Upendra Baxi praise the Court for deepening democracy and protecting citizens' rights, comparing its intervention to chemotherapy for carcinogenic politics.

pages.title: Critiques by Pratap Bhanu Mehta and Lavanya Rajamani
pages.summary: Pratap Bhanu Mehta critiques the Supreme Court as a paradoxical, politicized institution contributing to post-democracy, while Lavanya Rajamani notes it is ill-equipped for the roles it undertakes. Mehta and Devesh Kapur assess the Court's pivotal yet controversial role in sustaining liberal democratic institutions and the rule of law.

pages.title: Judicial record on liberties and Mehta's critique
pages.summary: While the Supreme Court is credited with advancing substantive justice in health and education, it has faced criticism regarding preventive detention and free speech restrictions. Pratap Bhanu Mehta argues that the judiciary has expanded beyond its constitutional powers and creates uncertainty because decisions are artifacts of individual judges.

pages.title: Mehta on politicisation and judicial governance
pages.summary: Pratap Bhanu Mehta asserts that judicial decisions represent delicate political balancing rather than legal principles, resulting in politicisation of the judiciary and judicial governance. He notes that the judiciary has expanded its power and popularity by stigmatizing the executive, with judicial activism yielding little real change in the quality of life.

pages.title: Upendra Baxi defense and landmark cases
pages.summary: Prof. Upendra Baxi defends the judiciary in 'Unfair to Justices', arguing that it has deepened democracy and protected the liberal order despite occasional flaws. Landmark cases such as Kesavananda Bharati and Maneka Gandhi are highlighted for safeguarding the Constitution's basic structure and establishing due process of law.

pages.title: Public Interest Litigation and judicial activism concept
pages.summary: The Supreme Court instituted Public Interest Litigation under Article 39(A) to ensure equal justice and free legal aid. Activism is defined using a chemistry analogy of electrons jumping orbits, describing judicial activism as the judiciary exceeding its mandate to intervene in executive and legislative spheres.

pages.title: Factors and Conditions for Judicial Activism
pages.summary: This page outlines the general conditions and unique Indian factors that give rise to judicial activism. It also introduces the idea that judicial activism must be differentiated from judicial review.

pages.title: Judicial Review, Judicial Activism, and Judicial Overreach
pages.summary: The page contrasts judicial review with judicial activism, citing the Kesavananda Bharati case and the invalidation of the 99th Constitutional Amendment as examples. It further explains the subjective distinction between judicial activism and judicial overreach based on public consent.

pages.title: Judicial High-Headedness and Conventional Perspectives on Activism
pages.summary: The page explains judicial high-handedness using the example of contempt notices against journalists to protect erring judges. It also presents the conventional school of thought, where Lord Jowett, Justice Bharucha, and Justice M. Katju argue against judges making laws or micromanaging administration.

pages.title: Contemporary Views and Desirability of Judicial Activism
pages.summary: The page details the contemporary school supporting judicial activism, citing Justice Reed, Justice P.N. Bhagwati, and Kalpana Kannabiran. It also notes the debate on its desirability in India, referencing critics like Manmohan Singh and supporters like Upendra Baxi.

pages.title: Role and Limits of Judicial Activism in India
pages.summary: The page describes judicial activism as a safety valve in India that protects constitutional sanctity, human rights, and fills policy gaps during parliamentary decline. It also references observations by Bhikhu Parekh and P.B. Mehta, concluding that judicial activism should be treated as medicine rather than daily bread.

flashcards.front: According to Lord Bryce, what is the ultimate test of the excellence of any government?
flashcards.back: According to Lord Bryce, there is no better test of the excellence of a government than the functioning of its judicial system. An efficient judiciary is an integral component of good governance, which is an essential pre-condition for economic development.

flashcards.front: Why did Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru assert that the Indian Constitution does not envisage a passive judiciary?
flashcards.back: Pandit Nehru maintained that the Indian Constitution envisions the judiciary as an active participant in India's social revolution. Following the 1947 political revolution, Granville Austin noted that India embarked on a social and economic revolution to transform traditional society into a modern society.

flashcards.front: How does Article 141 of the Constitution empower the Supreme Court to lay down binding law?
flashcards.back: Article 141 provides that the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India. This empowers the judiciary to declare law that operates as binding statute until the legislature enacts legislation, such as the Vishakha guidelines on workplace sexual harassment.

flashcards.front: What plenary power does Article 142 grant to the Supreme Court of India?
flashcards.back: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to issue any order or decree necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it. It places a constitutional obligation on the executive and legislative branches of government to implement these orders.

flashcards.front: Why does Upendra Baxi describe the Supreme Court's intervention as 'chemotherapy' for Indian politics?
flashcards.back: Upendra Baxi argues that the Supreme Court administers vital chemotherapy to treat the carcinogenic tendencies of Indian politics. By enforcing the rule of law and safeguarding citizens' fundamental rights, the Court has transformed into the trusted 'Supreme Court of Indians'.

flashcards.front: Why does Pratap Bhanu Mehta characterise the Indian judiciary as a 'self-perpetuating, paradoxical' institution?
flashcards.back: In 'India's Judiciary: The Promise of Uncertainty', Pratap Bhanu Mehta argues that while the Supreme Court sustains liberal democracy, its career is shadowed by irony and controversy. He critiques judicial rulings as unpredictable 'artifacts' of individual judges that engage in political balancing rather than adhering to consistent legal principles.

flashcards.front: How did Zia Mody assess the historical impact of the Basic Structure doctrine?
flashcards.back: Zia Mody observed that had the Supreme Court not formulated the Basic Structure doctrine in the Kesavananda Bharati case, democracy in India would not have survived. Without this judicial safeguard, India would have followed the path of other Third World nations where democracy collapsed into dictatorship.

flashcards.front: How is the concept of judicial activism illustrated through an analogy with chemistry?
flashcards.back: Judicial activism is compared to an electron in an atom that absorbs extra energy and jumps out of its assigned orbit into another orbit. Similarly, when an institution gains extra energy, exceeds its constitutionally mandated boundaries, and interferes in the spheres of the legislature or executive, it constitutes activism.

flashcards.front: What arguments did Lord Jowett, Justice Bharucha, and Justice Markandey Katju present against judicial law-making?
flashcards.back: Lord Jowett declared that it is indecent for judges to make laws. Justice Bharucha argued that the judiciary has neither the expertise nor resources to micromanage the administrative leviathan, while Justice Markandey Katju insisted that judges should declare existing law rather than create new law.

flashcards.front: In what context did judicial activism serve as a constitutional 'safety valve' in India?
flashcards.back: Judicial activism functioned as a safety valve when Parliament faced institutional decline and the executive acted arbitrarily or passively, leaving revolution as the only alternative for citizens. It protected constitutional sanctity, combated corruption, filled governance voids during policy paralysis, and advanced substantive rights like education and food.

answers.question: Critically examine the phenomenon of Judicial Activism in India. Has it functioned as an essential democratic safety valve or crossed into judicial overreach?
answers.intro: Judicial activism represents the judiciary exceeding its mandated sphere to intervene in legislative and executive domains. In India, institutional passivity and executive overreach transformed judicial intervention into an indispensable mechanism to uphold constitutionalism and human rights.
body: Prof. Upendra Baxi defends judicial activism as vital chemotherapy for India's carcinogenic politics, highlighting that landmark verdicts in Kesavananda Bharati and Maneka Gandhi protected constitutional sanctity, introduced due process, and expanded basic socio-economic rights through Public Interest Litigation.

Contemporary jurists including Justice P.N. Bhagwati, Justice Reed, and Kalpana Kannabiran reject pedantic legalism, maintaining that legal interpretation is always a creative act and that judicial passivity constitutes an abdication of constitutional duty when basic rights are violated.

Conversely, conventional jurists like Lord Jowett, Justice Bharucha, and Justice Markandey Katju critique judicial overreach, asserting that the judiciary possesses neither technical competence nor administrative machinery to micromanage executive policy, exemplified by contentious directives on inter-state river linking.

Pratap Bhanu Mehta, writing with Devesh Kapur, alongside Bhikhu Parekh, warns that activism fosters post-democracy and judicial co-governance, wherein unpredictable judgments become personal artifacts of individual judges that stigmatize the executive without yielding real qualitative life improvements.
answers.conclusion: Judicial activism has served as a valuable constitutional safety valve preventing systemic collapse during executive inertia. However, as cautioned in the notes, judicial activism must remain a remedial medicine rather than becoming the daily bread of governance.

answers.question: Why does Pratap Bhanu Mehta characterise the Supreme Court of India as a 'paradoxical institution'? Critically evaluate its constitutional performance.
answers.topic: Constitutional Role and Paradoxes of the Supreme Court
answers.intro: The Supreme Court of India is globally recognized as an exceptionally powerful judicial body. However, as scholars highlight, its record displays profound paradoxes between safeguarding constitutional democracy and expanding its own institutional power beyond textual mandates.
body: Granville Austin and Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru envisioned the Supreme Court as an active participant in India's socio-economic revolution, a mandate realized through expansive interpretations of Article 36, Article 141, and Article 142 to secure substantive welfare rights.

Upendra Baxi in 'Unfair to Justices' and Zia Mody defend the judiciary for sustaining liberal democracy, arguing that preserving constitutional supremacy in Kesavananda Bharati and expanding fundamental liberties in Maneka Gandhi established the Court as an indispensable institution of public trust.

However, Pratap Bhanu Mehta and Devesh Kapur in 'Public Institutions in India' critique the Court as self-perpetuating and paradoxical, noting that while it proclaims constitutionalism, its rulings often reflect political balancing and unpredictable artifacts of individual judges.

Lavanya Rajamani contends that the judiciary prefers to undertake executive roles for which it is ill-equipped while neglecting its core adjudicatory functions, creating a regime of judicial governance where institutional power expands at the expense of parliamentary accountability.
answers.conclusion: Resolving the Supreme Court's institutional paradox requires reconciling judicial independence with democratic accountability. The judiciary must ground its interventions in enduring constitutional principles rather than ad hoc judicial governance, ensuring harmonious co-existence among the organs of state.
